concepts.title: Two-Component Cloning System and Vector Features

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Two-Component Cloning System and Vector Features' refers to.
questions.a: Gene cloning pairs a carrier with a workhorse: the insert is spliced into a vector, the recombinant DNA enters a host, and the host's enzymes multiply the construct; E. coli K12, doubling about every twenty minutes, leads the prokaryotic hosts with Bacillus subtilis for secreted proteins and yeast for eukaryotes, while a usable vector must stay small, carry an origin of replication, offer unique restriction sites and bear at least one selectable marker such as tetracycline or ampicillin resistance.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Two-Component Cloning System and Vector Features'.
questions.a: Host supplies the replication machinery, vector supplies the control sequences - and four features make a vector worth using.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Two-Component Cloning System and Vector Features' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'M13 Filamentous Phage Vectors' refers to.
questions.a: M13 threads a 6.4 kb single-stranded circular genome through a tube-shaped capsid, infecting only F-pilus-bearing E. coli without lysing them; inside, the strand becomes a double-stranded replicative form exploited for cloning inserts into the non-essential intergenic region, and vectors like M13mp18 add blue-white screening while yielding abundant single-stranded template.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'M13 Filamentous Phage Vectors'.
questions.a: Clone into the intergenic region of the replicative form and harvest single-stranded DNA from the medium without killing the host.

questions.q: Under which section is 'M13 Filamentous Phage Vectors' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Cosmids and Phasmids as Hybrid Vectors

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cosmids and Phasmids as Hybrid Vectors' refers to.
questions.a: Two hybrids stretch cloning capacity: a cosmid grafts as little as 250 bp of lambda DNA carrying the cos junction onto plasmid functions, letting recombinants of up to about 45 kbp be packaged in vitro into phage heads yet propagate as plasmids; a phasmid keeps whole lambda lytic genes at its ends around a central plasmid, replicating as a phage unless a lambda repressor gene flips it to plasmid mode.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cosmids and Phasmids as Hybrid Vectors'.
questions.a: Cos sites win phage packaging, plasmid ori wins propagation - combine both and large inserts travel either way.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cosmids and Phasmids as Hybrid Vectors' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Expression Vectors and Heterologous Expression' refers to.
questions.a: Expression vectors do more than carry DNA - an inducible promoter upstream, a ribosome binding site, unique insertion sites and a downstream terminator wrap the cloned gene into an expression cassette that the host transcribes and translates on command; eukaryotic genes expressed in prokaryotes must arrive intron-free and need no post-translational dressing such as glycosylation to work.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Expression Vectors and Heterologous Expression'.
questions.a: Promoter before, terminator after, inducible control throughout - and intron-free inserts when the host cannot splice.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Expression Vectors and Heterologous Expression' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Shuttle Vectors between Two Hosts' refers to.
questions.a: Shuttle vectors pack two origins of replication and dual selection systems so one construct lives in E. coli for engineering and in yeast, plant or animal cells for expression, with only one origin active in any given host; most eukaryotic vectors are in fact such shuttles built by recombinant DNA methods.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Shuttle Vectors between Two Hosts'.
questions.a: Two origins, two markers, one plasmid - build in bacteria, express in the eukaryote.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Shuttle Vectors between Two Hosts' taught, and from which source text?
